body_text: Offering nearly 3 MWh of energy with up to 7 MW of continuous power for demanding data center, AI infrastructure and critical-power applications Initial deliveries targeted for Q2 2027 from Electrovaya’s Jamestown, NY manufacturing facility, designed to support 48E Investment Tax Credit eligibility Electrovaya Inc. (“Electrovaya” or the “Company”) (Nasdaq: ELVA; TSX: ELVA), a leading lithium-ion battery technology and manufacturing company, today announced the launch of ElvaPulse™ 1500, a new high-power stationary battery energy storage system (“BESS”) platform. Artificial intelligence is reshaping data center power demand, which the International Energy Agency projects will more than double by 2030. AI workloads draw power unevenly, with frequent, large surges that put facility uptime at risk. Meeting that challenge requires storage designed to deliver large bursts of power on demand. ElvaPulse™ 1500 was purpose-built to close that gap. ElvaPulse™ 1500 is the first product introduced under Electrovaya’s new ElvaPulse stationary energy storage portfolio. This product leverages the proprietary ceramic separator design underpinning Electrovaya’s Infinity Battery Technology, which has been validated across more than 30,000 battery systems operating in demanding industrial environments. The family is being developed for demanding applications where enhanced safety, rapid power delivery, frequent cycling, and long operating life are essential, including AI and data center infrastructure, resilient microgrids, industrial power management, critical backup power, peak-demand management and renewable-energy firming. Built around a modular 20-foot container and a 1500 VDC architecture, ElvaPulse 1500 provides up to 2.88 MWh of nominal energy capacity and can be configured to deliver up to approximately 7 MW of continuous power with industry leading cycle life. This power-to-energy ratio allows ElvaPulse 1500 to discharge its full rated capacity in under 30 minutes — well above the roughly 2- to 4-hour duration profile of most utility-scale lithium-ion BESS platforms on the market today. Electrovaya believes this makes ElvaPulse 1500 one of the highest power-density containerized stationary battery systems commercially available. That power density translates into a smaller site footprint and lower balance-of-system costs relative to lower-power-density alternatives. “Data centers and other mission-critical facilities are pushing the energy storage industry toward higher and higher power delivery, and ElvaPulse 1500 was purpose-built to meet that need,” said Raj DasGupta, Chief Executive Officer of Electrovaya. “With up to 7 MW of continuous power from a single 20-foot container, ElvaPulse 1500 offers the highest power density available in a stationary lithium-ion platform today, while bringing the proven safety and longevity of our Infinity Battery Technology to these demanding applications. We designed this platform to give customers the flexibility to configure power, runtime and footprint around their specific requirements.” Electrovaya has initiated certification activities for ElvaPulse 1500 under UL 1973 and UL 9540, with completion currently targeted for the first quarter of CY-2027. The Company is already in active discussions with hyperscale and energy developers on ElvaPulse deployments, and is accepting production reservations now, with initial deliveries targeted to begin in the second quarter of CY-2027 from its Jamestown, New York manufacturing facility. The ElvaPulse platform is designed to support customer eligibility for the Section 48E Investment Tax Credit, including the domestic content bonus credit and compliance with Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) material assistance requirements under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, subject to project-specific structuring and each customer's own tax position. Electrovaya will showcase the ElvaPulse 1500 at three upcoming industry events: ACP RECHARGE: Energy Storage Conference, September 22–24 in Aurora, Colorado; Yotta 2026, September 28–30 in Las Vegas, Nevada; and RE+ 26, November 16–19 in Las Vegas, Nevada. Electrovaya representatives will also participate in speaking sessions addressing high-power energy storage and emerging critical-power applications. title: Do GLP-1 Medications Cause Hair Loss? The Link Between Weight Loss and Shedding
summary: You're committed to making healthy changes to yourself. You started a GLP-1 medication, your appetite changed, the weight began to move, but then a few months later, your hair starts showing up everywhere: in the shower, in your brush, and on your pillow. That kind of shedding can feel personal, especially when you are doing something positive for your health. So it is natural to ask: do GLP-1 medications cause hair loss? The good news is that current evidence does not clearly show that GLP-1 medications directly damage hair follicles. Instead, rapid weight loss, lower food intake, and nutrient changes can place stress on the body, which may push more hairs into the resting phase. Doctors often evaluate this kind of diffuse shedding as possible telogen effluvium, a common and usually temporary type of shedding that can happen after major changes like weight loss, illness, surgery, stress, or hormonal changes. This kind of shedding is often a sign that your body and scalp need support, not a sign that your hair is gone for good. GLP-1 Hair Loss Is Usually Linked to Weight Loss, Not Follicle Damage GLP-1 medications are used to support blood sugar management, weight management, and certain cardiometabolic health goals, depending on the specific prescription and patient need. Hair loss is not commonly framed as direct follicle damage in this context, although some patients still report shedding during a GLP-1 routine. That can feel confusing. Your experience can still be real even when hair loss is not considered a common listed side effect for every GLP-1 medication. More likely, the link between GLP-1 medications and hair shedding is indirect. When someone eats less, loses weight quickly, or gets less protein and key nutrients during treatment, the body may respond to that change as stress. More hairs can move into the resting phase, and a few months later, those resting hairs may shed at the same time. GLP-1 Medications Do Not Appear to Attack Hair Follicles Directly Current evidence does not clearly show that GLP-1 medications directly damage the follicle. In many cases, the follicle is still active beneath the surface. It may simply be resting. That's important because resting follicles can often return to the growth phase once the body stabilizes. Most GLP-1-Related Shedding Is Temporary Hair shedding can feel alarming, but it does not automatically mean permanent hair loss. Many cases that fit telogen effluvium improve once the trigger settles and the body receives consistent support. Talk with your prescribing clinician before changing any GLP-1 medication. Then review your nutrition, watch for other symptoms, and support your scalp with a gentle, consistent routine. How Weight Loss on GLP-1 Medications Can Affect the Hair Cycle Hair follicles are sensitive to change. They rely on steady nutrition, energy, and internal balance to keep producing strong, healthy-looking strands. Telogen effluvium happens when more hairs than usual move into the resting phase of the hair cycle. This can happen after weight loss, illness, surgery, stress, hormonal changes, medication changes, or a major diet change. With GLP-1 medications, the trigger may be the change happening around treatment: less food, faster weight loss, and lower intake of nutrients that help support normal hair growth. Here is the simple version: Appetite drops or weight changes quickly. The body experiences internal stress. More follicles move into the resting phase. Two to four months later, those resting hairs shed together. Lower Appetite Can Mean Lower Hair-Supportive Nutrition Many people eat less during GLP-1-supported weight loss, especially when fullness comes sooner or meals become smaller. When food intake drops sharply, protein and micronutrient intake may drop too. Hair production is an active biological process. Your follicles need consistent support from nutrients like protein, iron, B vitamins, vitamin D, and zinc. Nutrient gaps do not cause every case of hair loss, but low protein intake, low iron stores, and certain vitamin or mineral deficiencies may contribute to shedding for some people. Nutrient Why Hair May Need It What You Should Do Protein Supports keratin production Ask about daily protein targets Iron / Ferritin Supports oxygen transport and growth processes Discuss labs if hair shedding is heavy B12 Supports red blood cell and nerve function Discuss testing if intake is low or fatigue is present Vitamin D Associated with hair and immune function Ask about testing if deficiency risk is high Zinc Supports tissue repair and growth Avoid high-dose supplementation without guidance A clinician can help you decide whether lab testing makes sense. GLP-1 Hair Loss Often Shows Up Months Later One of the most confusing parts of GLP-1-related hair loss is the timing. You may feel fine at first. Your appetite changes. Your weight begins to move. Then, a few months later, the hair shedding becomes hard to miss. Some people may also notice a wider-looking part line or more visible thinning around the crown, especially in certain lighting. Signs Your Shedding May Fit Telogen Effluvium Shedding started 2 to 4 months after weight loss or appetite change. Hair falls from across the scalp rather than one patch. More strands appear in the shower, brush, or pillow. The scalp does not show scarring, pain, or severe inflammation. The part line or ponytail looks thinner than usual. If this sounds familiar, try not to panic. Look at the full picture: how quickly your weight changed, whether your protein intake dropped, whether nutrient levels may be low, and whether stress, styling habits, or hormonal changes may also be contributing. Your hair may be responding to a season of change. With the right support, your body and scalp can have a steadier foundation while the hair cycle recovers. Ozempic Hair Loss in Women: Hormones, Nutrition, and Scalp Support For many women, hair changes feel personal right away. A wider part line, a thinner ponytail, or more visible scalp at the crown can affect how you feel when you look in the mirror, even if the shedding is temporary. If you are trying to understand hair loss while taking a GLP-1 medication, it helps to look at the full picture. For women, hair shedding may be connected to weight changes, nutrition, hormones, stress, scalp health, or a combination of factors. Common overlapping triggers can include: Iron deficiency Thyroid changes Postpartum hair changes Perimenopause or menopause PCOS Stress Low protein intake Androgen-related thinning Tight hairstyles, extensions, or tension at the scalp Talk with a doctor or dermatologist if heavy hair shedding comes with fatigue, dizziness, brittle nails, irregular periods, cold intolerance, scalp pain, scaling, or patchy hair loss. Those signs may point to something beyond temporary shedding. Hair shedding is not your fault. A steady plan can support your body, protect your scalp, and give fragile hair the gentler care it needs while the hair cycle resets. How Long It Takes Hair to Recover After GLP-1 Shedding The hardest part of GLP-1-related hair shedding is that it rarely follows the timeline you expect. You may already feel settled into your medication routine when the hair shedding suddenly becomes noticeable. The encouraging part is that this type of shedding is often temporary. Once weight loss slows, nutrition becomes more consistent, and the body feels less stressed, the hair cycle can begin to steady itself. Shedding may improve before full density returns, so patience matters. Phase Possible Timing What You May Notice Trigger Weeks 1 to 12 Appetite drops, weight changes, or nutrient intake changes Onset Months 2 to 4 More hair appears in the shower, brush, or pillow Peak Months 4 to 6 The part line, crown, or ponytail may look thinner Stabilization Months 6 to 9 Shedding may slow as weight and nutrition stabilize Regrowth Months 9 to 12+ Short new hairs may appear, and density may gradually improve Visible recovery takes time because hair grows slowly. Even after shedding slows, it may take several months for new growth to make hair feel fuller again. Diffuse shedding can fit telogen effluvium, but patchy loss, scalp pain, scaling, scarring, or shedding that lasts beyond six months should be reviewed by a medical professional. How to Care for Your Hair and Scalp While Taking GLP-1 Medications When hair shedding feels sudden, it is completely understandable to try a proactive approach to resolve it, especially when your hair feels more fragile than usual. A supportive approach starts with a steady plan: help your body get the nutrients it needs, protect your scalp, and reduce unnecessary stress on shedding-prone hair. No shampoo, supplement, or scalp treatment can promise to stop GLP-1-related shedding overnight. But a thoughtful routine can help you care for your scalp, reduce visible breakage, and support healthier-looking hair while the hair cycle stabilizes. Start With the Nutrients Your Hair Depends On Hair growth is an active process, so your body needs consistent support while weight and appetite are changing. If shedding feels heavy or prolonged, ask your clinician whether it makes sense to review protein intake, iron and ferritin, vitamin B12, vitamin D, zinc, thyroid function, weight-loss speed, and other medications or health changes. This matters even more if shedding comes with fatigue, dizziness, brittle nails, cold intolerance, or other symptoms. Keep Your Scalp Routine Gentle and Consistent GLP-1-related shedding often begins inside the body, but your daily hair-care routine happens at the scalp. Scalp care cannot replace nutrition or medical guidance. Still, a gentle routine can help create a cleaner, more balanced environment for healthier-looking hair while your body adjusts. A scalp-supportive routine can help remove buildup without over-stripping, keep the scalp feeling clean, support the look and feel of stronger hair, reduce visible breakage, and limit stress from harsh cleansing, tight styles, or aggressive brushing. Make Small, Steady Changes Instead of Starting Over When hair is shedding, it can be tempting to try every product, supplement, or styling change at once. Too many changes can make it harder to know what is helping. A simpler routine is often better. Focus on internal support, gentle scalp care, low-tension styling, and medical guidance when needed. That daily routine can become a steady, supportive step while your body adjusts. Reviv3 does not replace medical care, nutrition support, lab testing, or guidance from your GLP-1 prescriber. Instead, Reviv3 helps you build a simple scalp-first routine that supports cleaner roots, healthier-looking strands, and a more consistent approach to hair care during shedding. Shop BOOST → Reviv3 can support scalp health, help strengthen the look and feel of hair, and help reduce visible breakage. GLP-1 Hair Loss Mistakes That Can Make Shedding Feel Worse GLP-1 hair loss can feel urgent, but sudden medication changes, crash dieting, over-supplementing, and aggressive hair routines can add more stress to an already sensitive hair cycle. Common Mistake Better Move Stopping GLP-1 medication suddenly Call your prescriber first Eating too little protein Ask about a realistic daily protein target Trying every hair product at once Build one consistent scalp-care routine Ignoring patchy or painful loss See a dermatologist Mega-dosing supplements Ask about labs and safe dosing Do not stop a GLP-1 medication without medical guidance. Medication decisions should consider blood sugar management, weight-management goals, cardiovascular risk, kidney health, and your overall medical history. Avoid crash dieting while your appetite is already lower. Very low food intake can add to the body stress that may contribute to shedding, especially if protein and key nutrients drop too quickly. Be careful with supplements, too. More is not always better. High-dose iron, zinc, vitamin D, or other hair supplements may be unnecessary or unsafe without lab guidance. When to See a Doctor About GLP-1 Hair Loss Many cases of GLP-1-related shedding are temporary, but you should not have to guess your way through it. If something feels unusual, a clinician can help you understand whether the shedding fits telogen effluvium or whether another factor may be involved. Talk to a medical professional if you notice: Patchy hair loss Scalp pain, redness, scaling, or scarring Shedding that lasts longer than six months Heavy shedding with fatigue or dizziness Brittle nails, cold intolerance, or heavy periods Signs of infection or inflammation Sudden worsening of hair density Patchy hair loss may point to alopecia areata, fungal infection, traction alopecia, or another scalp condition that needs a closer look. Diffuse shedding with fatigue, dizziness, or brittle nails may also be a reason to ask about lab testing for nutrient deficiencies, thyroid changes, or anemia. Common Questions About GLP-1 Hair Loss Do GLP-1 Medications Cause Hair Loss? Current evidence does not clearly show that GLP-1 medications directly target or damage hair follicles. However, GLP-1 medications may contribute to shedding indirectly when rapid weight loss, reduced food intake, or nutrient changes place stress on the body. Diffuse shedding in this context is often evaluated as possible telogen effluvium. Is Hair Loss a Side Effect of GLP-1 Medications? Hair loss is not listed as a common side effect for every GLP-1 medication. Still, some patients and clinicians report shedding in GLP-1 weight-loss contexts. Your shedding can be real even if it is not considered a common listed side effect. Can GLP-1 Medications Cause Hair Loss? GLP-1 medications may be associated with hair shedding in some patients, especially when weight changes happen quickly. The risk appears to be connected to weight-loss speed, lower food intake, nutrition changes, and individual health factors rather than direct follicle damage. How Long Does GLP-1 Hair Loss Last? GLP-1-related shedding may last several months, especially if weight loss is still happening quickly or nutrition remains low. Many cases that fit telogen effluvium improve once the body stabilizes, but visible regrowth often takes longer than the shedding itself. Will Hair Grow Back After GLP-1 Hair Loss? Hair often improves after telogen effluvium because the follicles are usually resting rather than permanently destroyed. Give the hair cycle time, and seek medical guidance if shedding is severe, patchy, painful, or lasts longer than expected. How Can Women Stop Hair Loss From GLP-1 Medications? Women can support hair during a GLP-1 routine by reviewing protein intake, asking a clinician about iron, thyroid, B12, vitamin D, or other relevant labs, reducing styling stress, and using a consistent scalp-care routine. Women should not stop a GLP-1 medication without guidance from their prescribing clinician. Can You Prevent Hair Loss While Taking GLP-1 Medications? You may be able to lower the risk of shedding by avoiding crash dieting, maintaining enough protein, asking about nutrient labs when appropriate, losing weight at a medically guided pace, and supporting scalp health consistently. GLP-1 Shedding Can Improve With Time, Nutrition, and Scalp Care GLP-1 hair loss can feel frustrating, especially when the shedding seems to appear out of nowhere. In many cases, it is more understandable than it first feels. Current evidence does not clearly show that GLP-1 medications directly damage hair follicles. More often, shedding is linked to the changes happening around weight loss and the stress those changes can place on the body. When more hairs move into the resting phase, visible shedding can show up a few months later. Steady support makes a meaningful difference. Work with your prescriber, review your nutrition, ask about lab testing if symptoms suggest a deficiency, and give your scalp a gentle routine that supports healthier-looking hair over time. Reviv3 fits into this plan as scalp and hair-care support, not as a replacement for medical care. title: EU's 21st Package Extends Crypto Sanctions to Third Countries
summary: The EU's 21st sanctions package bans 14 crypto platforms in third countries and adds power to sanction evasive jurisdictions. See what it means for compliance.
body_text: Key takeaways On July 23, 2026, the Council of the EU adopted its 21st sanctions package against Russia, extending transaction bans to 14 crypto-related service platforms and adding four designations tied to the A7 network. The package's 218 total listings are the largest batch in four years. For crypto compliance teams, the biggest change is a powerful new authority to ban crypto asset services from entire third countries when they facilitate Russian sanctions evasion. The designated platforms sit outside the EU in Georgia, Panama, the UAE, the Marshall Islands, Kyrgyzstan, and Belarus. The measures reach the infrastructure wherever it operates. The designations extend a wave of multilateral action against the Russia sanctions evasion network, following the UK's May 26, 2026 crypto designations of HTX, Exmo, Bitpapa, Rapira, and others. A designation names an entity; it does not reveal the wallets that entity controls today. Blockchain intelligence closes that gap by tracing a designated platform through wallet changes to the addresses it uses now. ‍ {{horizontal-line}} The EU pushes its crypto sanctions past its own borders The European Union adopted its 21st package of restrictive measures against Russia on July 23, 2026, targeting the energy, financial services, crypto, and trade sectors in a single round of 218 listings — 48 individuals and 170 entities, the largest batch in four years. The change that matters most for crypto compliance teams is the package's reach beyond the bloc. Earlier rounds named platforms one at a time; this one extends transaction bans to platforms in third countries and creates a new power to ban crypto asset services from entire third countries when they facilitate Russian sanctions evasion. Russia's access to the international financial system now runs through a network of intermediaries built to survive the loss of any single node, and much of it operates well outside the EU. What the Council adopted on July 23 The package expands EU action against Russia's financial and banking sector alongside its crypto measures. The Council imposed asset freezes and a prohibition on making funds available to 94 banks and major financial institutions, extended its transaction ban to 33 additional Russian credit and financial institutions, and added a transaction ban against a Kyrgyz bank connected to the SPFS financial messaging system plus three other non-Russian banks for circumventing sanctions. On crypto, the package does two things. It adds four designations tied to the cross-border A7 network, including its new links to Africa. It also extends the EU's transaction ban to 14 crypto-related service platforms based in Georgia, Panama, the UAE, the Marshall Islands, Kyrgyzstan, and Belarus. Kaja Kallas, High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy and chair of the Foreign Affairs Council, tied the crypto measures to the broader effort: "With each round of sanctions, we squeeze Russia's economy and its capacity to prolong its illegal war. Our 21st package includes the highest number of listings in four years. We're hitting over a hundred banks and crypto operators, 40+ vessels in Russia's shadow fleet, and several oil refineries in Russia and Belarus." The measures take effect under Council Regulation (EU) 2026/1844, which amends Regulation (EU) No 269/2014, alongside the accompanying decisions and Belarus-mirroring acts. The Council noted that the relevant legal acts will be published shortly in the Official Journal of the EU. A country-level ban is a new kind of tool Earlier crypto measures froze a named platform. The third-country provision works at a different level: it lets the EU cut off crypto asset services tied to an entire jurisdiction found to host platforms that serve Russia. The European Commission framed the intent as "a strong deterrent to countries hosting platforms that help Russia evade EU sanctions," and the provision would let the EU ban any transaction between an EU operator and a crypto provider used by Russia. That puts the compliance burden on the jurisdiction that tolerates the infrastructure and on the firms that transact with providers based there. A country that hosts sanctions evasion platforms now carries the risk that its crypto sector loses access to the EU market. The platforms the EU designated The crypto designations target platforms tied to the A7 sanctions evasion network, and several of the named entities were already designated by the United Kingdom or the United States. TRM has identified the following platforms and entities connected to the crypto and A7 network measures: Rapira — also designated by the UK Aifory Pro (Sooty Ltd.) — also designated by the UK ABCeX (Nueva Cryptologia S.A.S DE C.V.) — also designated by the UK WhiteBird NoOnecrypto INC. Tradex (Brightum LLC) Monease Ltd BitPapa — also designated by the US and the UK Exnode / Exnode Pay (Arvix) — also designated by the UK HTX (Huobi Global SA) — also designated by the UK EXMO Ltd — also designated by the UK A7 Nigeria A7 Africa PilotFinance Ltd The overlap with prior UK and US action is the through-line. These are not isolated targets, but nodes in the same network that allied jurisdictions have been designating in sequence. This extends the multilateral squeeze on the A7 network The EU's crypto designations build on recent multilateral action against the A7 network. The clearest precedent is the United Kingdom's May 26, 2026 action, which designated 18 entities and individuals — including Huobi Global (HTX), Exmo, Bitpapa, and Rapira — for their role in Russian sanctions evasion, and marked the first time the UK applied Regulation 17A of the Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019 to a crypto exchange. The pattern is by now familiar. When the United States and allies took down Garantex in March 2025, the flows it carried moved to successor infrastructure rather than stopping, and the A7 network — a set of entities, exchanges, and a ruble-pegged stablecoin tied to sanctioned Russian interests — absorbed much of that activity. Each designation cycle pushes flows toward the next node, which is why coordinated action across the UK, the US, and now the EU reaches more of the network than any single body can on its own. Designations name entities, wallets rotate The HTX case shows what happens after a major designation. Following the UK action, HTX kept operating under the same brand and rebuilt its on-chain plumbing, rotating deposit and hot wallets on regular cycles across TRON, Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain, and Solana. TRM analysis found the exchange retiring hot wallets and funding addresses within hours — a moving target that a static block list cannot keep pace with. That behavior is why a designation, on its own, does not tell a compliance team which wallets an entity controls today. Every wallet rotation, new deposit address, and transfer to a downstream service is visible and traceable, so a designated platform can be followed through its wallet changes to the addresses it is using now — not the ones it used on the day of the designation. What this means for compliance teams Screen the updated EU list now, and treat entity names as the starting point rather than the finish line. Funds one or two hops from a designated platform can still carry sanctions risk, and successor infrastructure absorbs flows as soon as a node is named — so monitoring for wallet rotation and downstream exposure matters as much as matching the list itself. The third-country provision is a new kind of tool. When the EU can act against a jurisdiction's entire crypto sector, firms will need to understand their exposure not only to the platforms named today, but to the jurisdictions that host them. Screening that layers behavioral signals on top of static list matching is what catches successor-flow patterns before the next designation cycle. ‍ {{horizontal-line}} Frequently asked questions (FAQs) 1. What does the EU's 21st sanctions package do on crypto? It extends EU transaction bans to 14 crypto-related service platforms based in third countries — Georgia, Panama, the UAE, the Marshall Islands, Kyrgyzstan, and Belarus — that service sanctioned Russian entities or help circumvent EU measures, adds four designations tied to the A7 network, and introduces a first-ever power to ban crypto asset services from a third country that hosts such platforms. 2. What is the third-country crypto ban? It is a new power that lets the EU cut off crypto asset services tied to a jurisdiction found to host platforms that help Russia evade sanctions, rather than designating those platforms individually. The Commission framed it as a deterrent to the countries that host such infrastructure, and it would let the EU ban any transaction between an EU operator and a crypto provider used by Russia. 3. Which platforms were designated? The named platforms include HTX (Huobi Global), EXMO, BitPapa, Rapira, Exnode, Aifory Pro, ABCeX, and others, alongside A7 Nigeria and A7 Africa. Many were previously designated by the UK or the US, reflecting the multilateral effort against the same network. 4. How does this connect to the A7 network and the UK's HTX designation? The EU designations extend multilateral pressure on the A7 sanctions evasion network. The UK designated HTX and 17 other entities on May 26, 2026 for the same nexus, and the US takedown of Garantex in March 2025 set off the successor flow pattern the network was built to absorb. 5. What should compliance teams do now? Screen the updated EU list, map indirect counterparty exposure within one to two hops of the designated platforms and the A7 network, and monitor for wallet rotation and successor infrastructure rather than relying on static entity matching alone. ‍ {{horizontal-line}} Methodology TRM attributes entities and addresses to real-world actors using on-chain analysis combined with open-source and proprietary intelligence. Flow figures, where cited, reflect direct on-chain transfers unless otherwise noted, and are reported in adjusted USD at the time of transaction. TRM's attribution database is being updated to reflect today's designations; TRM will continue to investigate and add any additional addresses as they are found.

title: Your chatbot answers questions. An AI agent resolves them — Curacel Support AI
body_text: When the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau reviewed chatbots in consumer finance, it found customers trapped in what it called “doom loops”: repetitive answers, no resolution, and no reliable path to a human. That is not only a conversation problem. It is an operations problem. A chatbot can explain how a process works. An AI support agent can use approved tools to move a verified request toward a real outcome. The difference is not better conversation. It is safe action. A Good Answer Can Still Leave the Customer Stuck Ask a traditional chatbot, “Where is my claim?” and it may explain where claims are normally tracked. It may provide a portal link or repeat a policy. The answer can be accurate and still leave the customer stuck. The CFPB found that financial-services chatbots could handle basic questions but often lost value as problems became more complex. Customers struggled when an issue required investigation, recognition of a dispute, an operational change, or a clean handoff to a person. An answer informs the customer. Resolution moves the request forward. An answer informs the customer. A support agent moves the request to the next safe step. What an AI Support Agent Actually Does OpenAI describes agents as systems that can direct a task and use tools. Some tools retrieve information. Others perform an approved action, such as updating a record, sending a message, or handing a ticket to a human. In customer support, that can mean: verifying the customer before opening account-specific information; retrieving a permitted policy, payment, or claim record; identifying what is blocking the request; completing a routine action within clear limits; and escalating the case with enough context for a person to continue. Consider a customer asking why a claim has not moved. An answer-only chatbot may direct them to a portal. An agent can verify the customer, retrieve the live status, identify a missing document, send an approved upload request, record the action, and confirm the next expected update. Anthropic recommends using the simplest system that works. Predictable support tasks may follow a fixed path. More complex cases need tighter limits and a human checkpoint. Four Guardrails Before It Acts Useful action needs control. Verify. General information may be public, but claim, policy, account, and payment details require the right identity checks. Limit. The agent should only access approved data and perform permitted actions. Record. Every retrieval, update, message, and handoff should leave a clear audit trail. Escalate. Complaints, vulnerable-customer cases, large financial changes, and exceptions should move to an authorised person. The handoff should include the conversation summary, relevant records, actions already attempted, and the reason a person is needed. The customer should not have to start again. NIST's Digital Identity Guidelines support keeping authentication separate from the application using it. The language model should never guess who the customer is. Useful automation is bounded by identity checks, permissions, audit logs, and human escalation. 👉 See how Curacel Support AI helps teams move customer requests from questions to safe next steps. Measure Resolution, Not Chatbot Volume Chatbot volume can look impressive while customers keep returning with the same problem. Better measures are: resolution rate for eligible requests; time to resolution; repeat-contact rate; and handoff quality. Human oversight still matters. The Bank of England and FCA's 2024 survey found that three in four responding financial firms already used AI, while only 2% of reported use cases involved fully autonomous decision-making. The right question is not, “How many conversations did the bot handle?” It is, “Did the interaction move the customer forward safely?” The Takeaway The next generation of customer support is not a chatbot with a more human tone. It is a controlled system that can verify, retrieve, act, record, and escalate. summary: Data Centers have become vital to our always-connected lives but are extremely vulnerable during seismic events. Learn how vibration control through a base isolation system can significantly reduce this risk.
body_text: One solution to keep the building from significant shaking is to install a Taylor-damped base isolation system. Similar to how shock absorbers work on your car when driving over a bumpy road, a base isolation system can absorb the energy from a seismic event as the building “floats” above the ground. By separating the structure from its base, the amount of energy that is transferred to the superstructure during an earthquake is reduced significantly. You can also add fluid viscous dampers to the base isolation system to significantly improve the performance and effectiveness of the isolators.
